The Minimax Principle

AlgebraLogicGame Strategy
Game: A table of numbers has its row smallest and column largest numbers written beside it (in blue). Then the biggest blue number at the side and the smallest blue number underneath are written in red. Compare the two red numbers.
How to play: Press Reset for new numbers. Press the left half of a number to make it smaller and the right half to make it bigger, to try to make the red numbers equal.

Press the left half of a number to lower it, the right half to raise it. With the keyboard use the arrow keys.

Look for the math

Call the smallest number in row i by Bi and the largest in column k by Ck. The blue numbers are the B's (at the right) and the C's (at the bottom). Then MaxMin = max Bi and MinMax = min Ck are the two red numbers. The statement behind the applet is the minimax principle for tables: MaxMin ≤ MinMax, and the two are equal exactly when some entry is the largest in its column and the smallest in its row (a saddle point).

Why MaxMin never exceeds MinMax

Take the column k₀ that gives MinMax, so MinMax = Ck₀, and any row i. The entry Ai,k₀ is at most Ck₀ (it is in the column) and at least Bi (it is in the row). So Bi ≤ Ai,k₀ ≤ MinMax for every row, and then the largest Bi, which is MaxMin, is at most MinMax. The test checked it on every table with up to 3 rows and 3 columns and entries up to 3 (262,144 for 3 by 3) and on 300,000 random tables.

When they are equal

If an entry is the largest in its column and the smallest in its row, it is at least Bi and at most Ck, so MinMax ≤ it ≤ MaxMin, and the two are equal. Conversely, if MaxMin = Bi₀ and MinMax = Ck₀ are equal, the entry Ai₀,k₀ is trapped between them and equals both. When they coincide, the page frames those entries: these are the saddle points. In the test the saddle points the page lists are exactly the entries that are both, and equality happened exactly when a saddle point existed, in every table tried.

Why it matters

In a two-player game where the table gives what one player pays the other, the row player can guarantee at least MaxMin and the column player can hold the loss to at most MinMax. With a saddle point both can stop worrying: this is the best that either can do. Without one (22% of the default 3 by 5 tables have one) the players need mixed strategies, a subject for game theory.

At 3 by 5, press Reset ten times. Then try to turn a table without a saddle point into one with a single change of one entry.
